outline.description: Sets out the facts leading to the felon-in-possession charge, the discovery and identification of the firearm, the trial results including the ACCA finding, the guideline calculation and sentence, and the issues raised on appeal.
subtopics: Offense conduct on November 19–20, 2020: paranoid behavior, closet confinement at gunpoint, threats, and striking D.F. with the firearm; involvement of D.F.’s children and housemate C.F.
Subsequent events: flight with D.F.’s phone and the gun; garage barricade; erratic claims of being armed; violent resistance including biting an officer and grabbing his gun

Recovery and identification of evidence: along the likely path, officers found the phone, a butcher knife, and a sawed-off Marlin .22 rifle; DNA on the rifle matched Cutbank; D.F. and C.F. recognized it from prior occasions
Charges and trial: § 922(g)(1) felon-in-possession; jury also found three or more prior violent felonies under § 924(e) (ACCA)
Verdict and sentence: guilty; PSR computed base level 26 (sawed-off firearm) plus enhancements; Criminal History Category VI; advisory range 292–365 months; 292 months imposed
Issues on appeal: multiple evidentiary/procedural challenges to the fairness of trial; challenge to application of USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) and overall reasonableness of the sentence

outline.chapter_title: Proving Possession: Intrinsic Evidence vs. Rule 404(b)
outline.description: Explains why testimony that D.F. and C.F. had previously seen Cutbank with the sawed-off rifle was admissible as intrinsic evidence directly probative of possession, not barred by Rule 404(b).
subtopics: Intrinsic evidence contrasted with Rule 404(b) propensity evidence: evidence that directly proves the charged offense is not “other-acts” evidence
Defense motion to exclude prior-sighting testimony; government’s theory of continuous possession of the same weapon
Eighth Circuit precedent: United States v. Battle—prior possession of the same firearm is directly relevant to later possession because it shows ownership/control
Application: D.F.’s testimony she saw the sawed-off rifle a “handful of times” before; C.F.’s similar testimony; district court’s pretrial and trial rulings admitting it
Standard of review (abuse of discretion) and the defendant’s failure to supply contrary authority on appeal

outline.chapter_title: Other Trial Rulings: Hearsay, Confrontation, Rule 403, and Impeachment Mechanics
outline.description: Analyzes the remaining evidentiary/procedural complaints: the denied request for an immediate limiting instruction, Confrontation Clause concerns, Rule 403 objections to brief testimony about a relative’s death, and the limits on impeaching a witness with a police report.
subtopics: Limiting instruction timing: court need not instruct contemporaneously if it provides appropriate instructions later (United States v. Bennett); officers’ testimony offered for context did not admit hearsay
Confrontation Clause satisfied where declarant (D.F.) testified and was subject to cross-examination (United States v. Charboneau)

Rule 403 challenge to D.F.’s statement that her sister was killed by a gun: arose on cross to explain inconsistencies; no unfair prejudice shown; similar remark by C.F. went unobjected; broad evidentiary discretion (e.g., Sprint/United Mgmt.)

Impeachment with a police report not authored by the witness: court allowed questioning about what C.F. told police but barred reading from the report absent authentication; extrinsic evidence of prior inconsistent statements must be authenticated (United States v. Cumbie)
Appellate briefing shortcomings (few citations/analysis) and the court’s admonition regarding needless expansion of issues by the government; effect on the scope and rigor of review

outline.chapter_title: Harmless and Cumulative Error: Why Any Alleged Missteps Did Not Matter
outline.description: Details the Eighth Circuit’s harmless-error and cumulative-error doctrines and applies them to conclude the evidentiary rulings did not affect the verdict given the government’s strong proof.
subtopics: Harmless error standard (United States v. DeMarce): reversal only if the jury may have been substantially swayed; slight influence is insufficient
Cumulative error limits (United States v. Keys): multiple harmless errors do not warrant reversal absent substantial prejudice
Application to this record: strong physical evidence (DNA on the firearm), recovery of the weapon and phone along the path, and consistent eyewitness identifications
Conclusion: no reversible evidentiary error; any assumed missteps were harmless and did not deny a fair trial

outline.chapter_title: Sentencing: The § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) Enhancement, ACCA Interplay, and Reasonableness Review
outline.description: Explains the four-level enhancement for possessing a firearm in connection with another felony, how the court relied on unobjected PSR facts, how ACCA interacts with the Guidelines, and why the within-range sentence was affirmed as reasonable.
subtopics: Guideline math from the PSR: base level 26 (sawed-off firearm), +3 (obliterated serial number), +2 (reckless endangerment during flight), +4 (§ 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) in connection with another felony); CHC VI; range 292–365 months

Scope of § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B): applies to use/possession in connection with any felony, whether or not separately charged (comment. n.14(C)); here supported by felonious conduct (e.g., domestic abuse/kidnapping/assault and injuring an officer) involving the gun
Factual basis and review: district court could adopt unobjected PSR facts; no clear error (United States v. Dunn)
ACCA interaction: jury’s ACCA finding triggers § 4B1.4; greater-of rule yields offense level 35 (from § 2K2.1 et al.) rather than 34 (from § 4B1.4(b))
Procedural reasonableness: correct Guidelines calculation is the starting point (Gall; Rosales-Mireles)

Substantive reasonableness: within-Guidelines sentences are presumed reasonable on appeal (United States v. Goodhouse); district court’s recognition and rejection of parsimony arguments after considering § 3553(a) (United States v. Masood; United States v. Maluoth); reasons included extensive violent criminal history and aggravated offense conduct
Holding: no procedural error, no abuse of sentencing discretion, and the 292-month within-range sentence is affirmed
